turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: ’Misfortunes,’ you call them? A convenient label, Mr. Darcy, to dismiss a man’s history without a shred of investigation! It appears you are as eager to judge as you are to pronounce yourself a benevolent friend.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I find myself at a distinct disadvantage, Miss Bennet, when my attempts at reasoned explanation are met with such… dismissiveness. It is exceedingly tiresome to be accused of superficial judgment when I possess a far deeper understanding of the matter than you appear to!

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Indeed, a deeper understanding? Pray tell, Mr. Darcy, what profound insights have you gleaned beyond your own self-satisfied pronouncements? It seems your ‘understanding’ consists solely of looking down upon those you deem less fortunate, and then declaring yourself superior for doing so.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Must I endure these accusations without the opportunity to defend myself, Miss Bennet? I assure you, my observations stem not from a desire for superiority, but from a conviction that proper judgment requires a consideration of circumstances beyond the superficial impressions you so readily embrace.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Circumstances, you say? Are you attempting to justify your interference in my sister’s happiness as a matter of ‘proper judgment,’ Mr. Darcy? I find it remarkably convenient that your ‘understanding’ always seems to align with your own preconceived notions and a desire to control the lives of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are, I confess, most unsettling. To suggest I desire control over another’s life is a gross misrepresentation of my intentions, and a rather impudent one at that, considering the delicate position in which I now find myself regarding *your* affections.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Imputent, am I? You speak of delicate positions, Mr. Darcy, yet it is *you* who has placed yourself in this awkward predicament with your unsolicited declarations and your tiresome attempts at justification! Do you truly believe I am so easily swayed by a few flattering words, or are you merely attempting to deflect from the undeniable truth of your own meddling?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your continued aspersions deeply wounding. To accuse me of meddling, of attempting to 'control' lives, is to demonstrate a profound lack of comprehension regarding my motivations, and a regrettable inclination toward rash judgment. I will not permit such baseless accusations to be levied against me without a proper and reasoned response.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A reasoned response? How very tiresome, Mr. Darcy. I assure you, I am perfectly capable of forming my own judgments, and I find your attempts at justification only serve to confirm my initial assessment of your character – an assessment I am increasingly reluctant to revise, despite your… unexpected declarations.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistence in this line of inquiry is, frankly, baffling. I have endeavored to explain my actions, to offer a glimpse into the reasoning behind them, yet you choose to interpret them through a lens of malice and presumption. I find myself increasingly at a loss to comprehend how to proceed when met with such unwavering and, dare I say, *unreasonable* resistance.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Unreasonable resistance? Pray, Mr. Darcy, do not mistake firmness for impropriety. I am merely exercising a faculty you seem to believe I lack: the ability to discern genuine benevolence from thinly veiled attempts at control, regardless of how passionately they are delivered.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words, while sharp, betray a certain…misunderstanding of my nature. I assure you, my intentions are not born of a desire for control, but rather of a profound and, I confess, overwhelming sense of… regard for your well-being, and a hope, however misguided, that you might one day reciprocate my sentiments.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Regard? Mr. Darcy, you mistake condescension for affection. To presume I require your protection, your *regard*, is an insult to my intelligence and a demonstration of precisely the arrogance I initially observed.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive your continued insistence upon misinterpreting my words and actions as a deliberate tactic. It is, I confess, most disheartening to find my sincerity so readily dismissed, yet I will not shrink from stating plainly: my regard for you is genuine, and it transcends any perceived condescension you might imagine.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Transcend perceived condescension, you say? How very generous of you, Mr. Darcy, to grant me such a charitable explanation for my continued disbelief. Pray, enlighten me further: do you truly expect me to accept this sudden outpouring of sentiment after years of barely concealed disapproval?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your skepticism is… predictable, given your established inclination towards distrust. However, to suggest I have *never* expressed approval would be a disservice to the truth; my silence was dictated by a consideration for propriety, a respect for your family’s standing, and a… a reluctance to impose upon you with sentiments I dared scarcely acknowledge even to myself.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Silence dictated by propriety? My dear Mr. Darcy, that is a convenient excuse for a man who has consistently demonstrated a decided lack of respect for both my family and myself. I find it exceedingly difficult to reconcile such a claim with your past behaviour, particularly your interference in my sister's happiness.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you wound me with such accusations! My interference regarding your sister was motivated solely by a desire to prevent a regrettable union, one that would undoubtedly have brought her unhappiness and disgrace. To characterize it as a 'lack of respect' is to fundamentally misunderstand my intentions, which, I assure you, were rooted in genuine concern.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Genuine concern? Mr. Darcy, you mistake paternalism for benevolence. My sister’s happiness is her own to determine, and your attempts to dictate her choices, cloaked in the guise of concern, only serve to highlight your arrogance and your condescending view of those less fortunate than yourself.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you persistently misinterpret my actions through a lens of prejudice! I acted with the utmost sincerity, believing I was safeguarding your sister from a disastrous match, and now you accuse me of paternalism and arrogance? I confess, I find your characterizations increasingly… vexing.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
